summary: Describes four optional security service extensions for S/MIME, which add extra features beyond basic signing and encryption, such as receipts and labels.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds four optional services to Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) email: signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing-list handling, and signing-certificate identification. Each adds information a recipient can check while processing a protected message.

subtitle: Four optional S/MIME services for receipts, message labels, mailing lists, and certificate binding.

tldr.problem: Basic S/MIME signing and encryption do not define signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing-list expansion, or a signed link to the certificate used for verification.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2634 defines attributes and procedures for those four services, including signed content identifiers, labels in signed attributes, expansion history, and certificate hashes.
tldr.outcome: The extensions add verifiable message-handling functions to S/MIME. RFC 2634 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 5035.

today: RFC 2634 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5035. The unit metadata does not list a later RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Four Optional S/MIME Services
sections.content:
Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME defines signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing lists, and signing certificates. The first three provide message-handling functions such as confirming receipt, marking sensitivity, and expanding encrypted mail for a list.

These extensions use signed attributes and message structures defined for S/MIME and CMS. Some features can make a message from a version 3 sender unreadable by a version 2 recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines four add-ons for signed and encrypted email. Mail software can use them to request a receipt, label content, handle mailing lists, or identify a signing certificate.

sections.title: Signed, Encrypted, and Signed Again
sections.content:
Some services use a triple-wrapped message: first signed, then encrypted, then signed again. The inner signature protects the original content and its attributes. Encryption protects the inner message, including those attributes. The outer signature authenticates the encrypted message and information processed by intermediaries such as mailing-list agents.

The RFC describes where attributes belong. For example, a receipt request is inner-only, while mailing-list expansion history is outer-only. Attributes defined by this RFC must be carried in the specified signed form and must not be duplicated in a signer record.
sections.plainLanguage: The inner signature protects the original message. Encryption hides it, and an outer signature protects information added while the encrypted message passes through intermediaries.

sections.title: Requesting and Verifying Signed Receipts
sections.content:
A signed receipt gives the sender evidence that a recipient could verify the original signature. The sender places a receiptRequest in the signed attributes of the innermost signature. It identifies the message, selects which recipients should return receipts, and lists receipt destinations. A receipt request cannot itself request another receipt.

A recipient must verify the signature covering the request before acting on it. To create the receipt, the recipient copies identifiers and the original signature value into a Receipt structure and signs the result, including a digest of the original signed attributes. The sender retains the original message or required digest values so it can validate returned receipts.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can ask recipients to return a signed record tied to the original message. A recipient checks the request first, then signs a receipt that lets the sender verify which message was received.

sections.title: Security Labels
sections.content:
A security label describes the sensitivity of protected content. A receiving agent can compare the label with a user's authorization; labels may also guide routing. The label includes a security-policy identifier and may include a classification, privacy mark, and security categories.

A label must be a signed attribute. If one signer in a SignedData object includes a label, all signers in that object must include an identical label. The policy identifier defines what the classification values mean. The RFC's basic hierarchy uses values 0 through 5, from unmarked to top-secret.

An equivalentLabels attribute can express a label under another policy. A receiver must ignore it when it understands the original label and must not use it unless the signature verifies and the signer is trusted to translate labels.
sections.plainLanguage: A security label describes how sensitive a message is under a named policy. Recipients must verify the signature before using the label to make an access decision.

sections.title: Secure Mailing Lists
sections.content:
A Mail List Agent (MLA) receives one message and performs recipient-specific processing before distributing it to list members. To detect loops between nested lists, it adds its identifier to the message's mlExpansionHistory attribute. If an MLA finds its own identifier in the history, it stops expanding the message and should alert an administrator. The history can hold at most 64 entries.

An MLA must verify and process security labels before distribution. It signs the outgoing message in a new outer SignedData layer and updates expansion history, without changing data protected by an inner signature. A list can set a receipt policy of none, insteadOf, or inAdditionTo; it cannot request receipts if the originator did not request them.
sections.plainLanguage: The mailing-list agent records which lists have already processed a message. If it sees itself in that record, it stops so the message does not circulate through the same lists again.

sections.title: Binding a Signing Certificate
sections.content:
The signingCertificate attribute binds a certificate identifier into the signed attributes. This addresses certificate substitution and reissue cases in which the certificate used to verify a signature might differ from the one the signer intended.

The first ESSCertID identifies the certificate used to verify the signature and includes a SHA-1 hash of the entire certificate. If that hash does not match, the signature is invalid. Additional identifiers can limit which authorization certificates are used during validation. The attribute itself must be signed.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer can include a fingerprint of the exact certificate intended for verification. If the receiver uses a different certificate, the signature check fails.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns against acting on receipt requests or security labels before verifying the signatures that cover them. A receipt can reveal information about the recipient, so senders should consider encrypting receipts. A security label alone does not force mail software to hide the message; a receiving agent that hides content must also prevent it from appearing in later error messages.

Mailing-list agents must consider risks from undecryptable messages and nested-list loops. Certificate verification should use certificates already known to be valid or identified by a signed SigningCertificate attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Recipients must verify signed attributes before relying on them. Labels and receipts provide information, but software must handle that information carefully to avoid exposing protected content.
